doc_summary: A METR RCT in which 16 experienced open-source developers completed 246 real issues in their own mature repositories with AI allowed or disallowed, finding a 19% slowdown despite expectations of speedup. The paper stresses real in-the-wild tasks, fixed outcome measures, and systematic checking of experimental artifacts over synthetic benchmarks and self-reports.

items.claim: Prefers real, in-the-wild tasks that participants would do anyway over synthetic or self-contained lab tasks, because synthetic tasks sacrifice realism and make it hard to infer real-world impact.
items.quote: tasks used in these lab experiments sacrifice realism for scale and efficiency: the tasks are typically self-contained, do not require much prior context/familiarity to understand and complete, and use algorithmic evaluation metrics which do not capture many important capabilities

items.claim: In a setup, use real work the participant genuinely wanted done (reviewed through the normal pipeline) instead of constructed tasks, because artificial tasks may resemble training data and unrepresentative work.
items.quote: Importantly, all issues represent real work that developers wanted to contribute to their repositories, and all work completed by developers is submitted and reviewed through each repository’s standard source-code management system

items.claim: In a setup, keep the subject's normal workflow and environment, minimizing deviations (and checking that the few deviations did not matter), instead of imposing a bespoke protocol, because behavior should match what happens outside the experiment.
items.quote: Contributors completed issues largely as they would outside of our experiment, with a few exceptions: they typically record their screen as they work

items.claim: In a setup, pay a flat hourly rate rather than per-task bonuses, because outcome-based incentives change behavior (splitting tasks, lowering quality) and bias what you are trying to observe.
items.quote: An alterative incentivization scheme could give developers bonuses for completed issues, to incentivize developers to work as quickly as possible. However, this could cause developers to break issues into smaller chunks

items.claim: Prefers outcome measures fixed before treatment assignment over measures the treatment can influence, because AI can change output metrics without changing real productivity.
items.quote: Crucially, the tasks are defined before they are randomized, limiting the impact of effects from AI assistance unrelated to productivity (e.g., more verbose but functionally equivalent code).

items.claim: Distrusts self-reports and expert forecasts of AI usefulness relative to measured behavior, because even after hours of use participants were miscalibrated about direction of effect.
items.quote: This underscores the importance of conducting field experiments with robust outcome measures, compared to relying solely on expert forecasts or developer surveys.

items.claim: When a surprising result appears, enumerate a priori hypotheses (especially experimental artifacts like awareness, cheating, dropout) and check each with multiple data sources, while cautioning against over-indexing on any single piece of evidence.
items.quote: Given the surprising nature of this result, we investigate 21 potential contributing factors that may contribute to developers spending more time on tasks when AI usage is allowed.

items.claim: Uses screen recordings to verify compliance and observe actual behavior (cheating, under-use) rather than trusting reported behavior, and acknowledges that non-blinding and awareness of being studied may change behavior.
items.quote: As this study is not blinded, developers’ awareness of the study may have changed their behavior.

items.claim: Prefers explicitly scoped claims with a list of what the evidence does not show over broad generalizations, because results are setting-specific and prone to misreading.
items.quote: We caution readers against overgeneralizing on the basis of our results. The slowdown we observe does not imply that current AI tools do not often improve developer’s productivity

items.claim: Tests robustness through alternative estimators, subsets excluding suspect data, and extreme-bias imputation simulations before accepting a result as not an artifact.
items.quote: this would represent a very extreme bias. When imputing using this extreme bias, we still do not observe substantial impacts on our speedup estimates in either case (14% and 23% slowdowns when using AI, respectively).

items.claim: Flags that elicitation with higher token spend, better scaffolding, and more AI experience may change the result and remains untested, and that learning effects need more research.
items.quote: Overall, it’s unclear how to interpret these results, and more research is needed to understand the impact of learning effects with AI tools on developer productivity.
